c.v: This stage turns the relay from a plain forwarder into a tool that can take odometry away from the supervisor on command, at a moment and for a length the bench chooses, and give it back by itself. The cue is a service, not Ctrl+C, because a service has an answer: the caller knows the relay heard it and until when the drop lasts.

The decision worth defending is that the drop's length is a duration, not a count of messages, so it can be compared directly against the supervisor's own timeout: a 2 s drop is eight timeouts whatever rate the odometry runs at, where "sixty messages" would mean something different on every robot. The window is half open too, from the cue up to but not including its end, so its length stays exact whichever moment within a cycle the cue lands on.
What we can now show: calling

in the running world makes the supervisor stop the robot about 250 ms later and start it again by itself once the drop ends, watched directly rather than inferred. Two tests prove the service is reachable and that a call really withholds messages for the length asked. And a drop shorter than the supervisor's own timeout leaves the robot driving straight through it, which is the exact relationship the next scenario turns into a number.

This is that topic, and the cue is what makes the next scenario possible: the bench has to take odometry away from the supervisor without touching the simulator or the bridge, at a moment it chooses, for a length it chooses, and then give it back.

Stopping the relay with Ctrl+C, which is what you did in the supervisor and frame topics, answers none of that. It needs a person at a keyboard, it happens at no particular moment, and the odometry never comes back, so a run can't check that the robot resumed. A drop with a cue and a length can be fired by the scenario runner and checked afterwards.

The length is a time and not a count of messages. The supervisor's rule is a timeout, 250 ms by default, so a drop measured in the same unit can be held against it: a 2 s drop is eight timeouts, and that stays true whatever rate the odometry runs at. A drop of "sixty messages" means eight timeouts on this robot and something else on the next one.

The window is half open, from the cue up to but not including its end. That keeps the length exact: a 2 s drop removes whatever arrived in a 2 s stretch, whether the first message lands on the cue or a millisecond after it. And the rule reads no clock. The caller passes the arrival time in, as
does, so a test pins the boundary to the nanosecond and the node decides which clock that is.

c.v: Four messages go missing, which at one message every 50 ms is exactly the 200 ms asked for. The message at 350 ms is forwarded: that is the half-open window, and it is why the count is four rather than five. The clock going back to 100 ms forwards, because 100 ms is before the cue, so a simulation that was reset or a bag that started again leaves the relay working rather than dropping until the end of time.
